# The gut microbiome

> *The colon holds a dense community of microbes that ferments what human enzymes cannot digest, and its
> products fuel the colonic lining and signal to the rest of the body. We cover how the microbiome is
> composed and develops, what it does for the host, how diet shapes it, and the clinical problems and
> marketing claims a doctor will meet, each judged by its mechanism and evidence.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Describe the composition of the adult gut microbiome and how it assembles from birth.
- Explain how colonic fermentation of fibre yields short-chain fatty acids, and where acetate,
  propionate and butyrate go.
- Explain why vitamins made by colonic microbes contribute little to the host's supply.
- Distinguish probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics and fermented foods by their consensus
  definitions.
- Recognise the one proven indication for faecal microbiota transplant, and refer.
- Evaluate common microbiome claims (test kits, cleanses, gut serotonin) by asking for the mechanism.
:::

## The gut microbiome at a glance {#sec-overview}

Food that escapes digestion in the small intestine is not wasted. The large intestine houses the
**gut microbiome**, a dense community of microbes (mostly bacteria, with some archaea, fungi and
viruses) that lives on what the small intestine could not digest and carries out chemistry that
human cells cannot.

The microbiome is best understood as an ecosystem: a community shaped by what it is fed, studied the
way an ecologist studies a habitat, with no single part to fix with a pill. It is also one of the most
heavily marketed topics in consumer nutrition. The mechanisms below are real and diet-modifiable; many
of the marketing claims do not survive the question "by what mechanism?"

## Composition and development of the gut microbiome {#sec-gut-who}

### Composition and abundance {#sec-composition}

The gut microbiome is a community of trillions of microbes, dominated by bacteria and concentrated in
the colon [@matijasic2020beyond].

::: {.concept-tree}
[Members of the gut microbiome]{.tree-title}

- Gut microbiome
  - Bacteria: dominant by mass and function
    - Bacillota (formerly *Firmicutes*)
    - Bacteroidota (formerly *Bacteroidetes*)
    - Actinomycetota, including *Bifidobacterium*
  - Archaea, including methanogens
  - Fungi: the **mycobiome**
  - Viruses: mostly **bacteriophages**, viruses that infect bacteria
:::

The phylum names were formally updated in 2021, so older papers use the former ones [@oren2021valid].

Microbial density climbs steeply along the gastrointestinal tract, and each region's conditions explain
its place on that gradient [@donaldson2016gutbiogeography]:

- In the stomach, acid keeps numbers low.
- In the small intestine, fast transit keeps numbers low.
- In the colon, slow transit, near-neutral pH and little absorption allow the highest density, by
  orders of magnitude, so the colon is the main site of microbial fermentation (see the
  [*Digestion and absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd) chapter).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do microbes outnumber human cells ten to one?
The figure of ten bacteria for every human cell is still widely quoted. It comes from a rough
estimate made in the 1970s. A 2016 recount put the ratio at roughly 1:1: about 38 trillion bacteria
to 30 trillion human cells, most of them (~84%) small red blood cells that the old estimate left out
[@sender2016revised]. The same recount puts total bacterial mass at about 0.2 kg; the often-quoted
"1–2 kg" conflates bacteria with the whole weight of the colonic contents.
:::

The collective microbial gene catalogue, the **metagenome**, is on the order of 150 times the ~20,000
genes of the human genome [@qin2010catalogue]. This "second genome" lets gut microbes extract energy and
make compounds that human cells cannot.

Two healthy people can carry very different species and still perform the same functions. This is
possible because each function, such as fibre fermentation, vitamin synthesis or short-chain fatty acid
production, is carried out by many different microbes, a property called **functional redundancy**
[@moya2016functional]. People therefore share a functional core more than a taxonomic one. Functional
redundancy also explains why **microbial diversity** (the number of species present and how evenly they
are represented) is only a loose health marker: a richer community tends to be more resilient, but there
are clear exceptions, so diversity is one context-dependent signal, not a number to maximise or to raise with
supplements [@mcburney2019healthy].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: what happened to "enterotypes"?
An older idea held that everyone belongs to one of three **enterotypes** (discrete community types). It
is now read as a continuous gradient [@knights2014rethinking].
:::

### How the microbiome develops {#sec-development}

The microbiome assembles over the first years of life and keeps shifting afterwards:

1. At birth, the gut is sparsely and erratically colonised, and delivery mode shapes the first
   community [@backhed2015dynamics].
2. In infancy, feeding is the more durable influence. Breast milk carries **human milk
   oligosaccharides (HMOs)**, sugars the infant cannot digest that selectively feed *Bifidobacterium*.
3. Weaning onto solids diversifies the community.
4. By about age three, after a gradual transition, the community is adult-like.
5. Late in life, in frailty and especially in institutional care, diversity tends to decline
   [@claesson2012elderly].

::: {.callout-note}
## Does caesarean birth permanently change the microbiome?
Infants born by caesarean section start with a different early community from infants born
vaginally, and this early difference is the source of the concern. The difference is largely
transient: feeding mode is the stronger and more durable influence, and the communities converge over the
first years. "Vaginal seeding" (swabbing a caesarean-born infant with vaginal fluid) is not an
evidence-based intervention and is advised against outside research, partly because of infection
risk [@acog2017vaginalseeding]. This evidence can relieve the guilt some parents feel after a
caesarean birth.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: two healthy adults carry very different gut species. Why can both still ferment fibre normally?
Fibre fermentation is carried out by many different microbes, so different species can perform the
same function (functional redundancy). The same property explains why a diversity count on its own is
only a loose marker of gut health.
:::

## What gut microbes do for the host {#sec-gut-function}

### Colonic fermentation and short-chain fatty acids {#sec-scfa}

Fermentation turns the fibre that human enzymes cannot digest into fuel for the colon. Three terms
describe the process:

Fermentation
: The anaerobic metabolism, by colonic bacteria, of food the host's enzymes could not digest. It
  differs from digestion, which is hydrolysis by the host's own enzymes in the small intestine
  [@koh2016scfa].

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs)
: The main products of fermentation: acetate, propionate and butyrate.

Colonocytes
: The epithelial cells lining the colon.

Human enzymes cannot break down dietary fibre or resistant starch, so both reach the colon undigested
(see the [*Digestion and absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd) chapter). There, anaerobic bacteria ferment
them into SCFAs, which fuel the colonocytes and act as signals elsewhere in the body. For the host, this
is a major function of the microbiome. Step through the pathway below, from what arrives in the
colon to where each product goes.

<div data-island="scfa-flow" data-src="/diagrams/scfa-flow.yml"></div>

The three SCFAs differ by only one or two carbons, but each goes to a different place
[@cummings1987scfa; @roediger1982colonocyte; @donohoe2011butyrate]:

| SCFA | Carbons | Share (approx.) | Where it goes | What it does there |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Acetate | 2 | 60% (most abundant) | Systemic circulation | Fuel for peripheral tissues and other bacteria |
| Propionate | 3 | 20% | Liver, via the portal vein | Substrate for gluconeogenesis (see the [*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd) chapter) |
| Butyrate | 4 | 20% (least abundant) | Stays in the colon | Main fuel of the colonocytes |

The 60:20:20 ratio varies with diet, substrate and site. Rotate the three molecules below to compare
their chain lengths.

<div data-island="molecule" data-src="/structures/scfa.mol.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-important}
## Is butyrate the most abundant SCFA?
Because butyrate is the most discussed of the three, it is easy to assume it is also the most
abundant. It is the least abundant, yet it is the main fuel of the colonic epithelium. Oral butyrate
supplements are mostly absorbed before they reach the colon, so claims that butyrate pills cure
disease run ahead of the evidence.
:::

Fermentation also produces gas, the source of the bloating described in the *Digestion and absorption*
chapter. Alongside the SCFAs, it releases three gases:

- hydrogen (H₂);
- carbon dioxide (CO₂);
- methane (CH₄), in people who carry **methanogenic archaea** (archaea that produce methane) such as
  *Methanobrevibacter smithii*, which consume H₂ and so let fermentation continue
  [@chaudhary2018methanogens].

More gas is produced when a large load of fermentable substrate arrives at once (undigested lactose,
beans, onions or certain **FODMAPs**, the fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides
and polyols), and the distension is felt as bloating and flatulence. Gas is usually a sign that
fermentation is proceeding normally.

A diverse microbiome is resilient partly because microbes **cross-feed**: one species lives on the
products of another. Many butyrate producers cannot break down fibre themselves, so they depend on
primary degraders such as *Bifidobacterium*, which ferment fibre into lactate and acetate. Butyrate
producers such as *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii* and *Roseburia* then convert those intermediates to
butyrate. A diverse range of fibres therefore feeds a diverse community [@riviere2016crossfeeding].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-crossfeeding
%%| fig-cap: "Cross-feeding: many butyrate producers cannot break down fibre themselves and live on what the primary degraders release. A diversity of fibres feeds a diversity of microbes."
flowchart LR
  F["Dietary fibre +<br/>resistant starch"] --> PD["Primary degraders<br/>(e.g. Bifidobacterium)"]
  PD --> INT["Lactate + acetate"]
  INT --> BP["Butyrate producers<br/>(F. prausnitzii, Roseburia)"]
  BP --> BUT["Butyrate<br/>→ fuels the colon lining"]
```

SCFAs also protect the gut wall in two ways: they lower colonic pH, which discourages acid-sensitive
pathogens, and butyrate fuels the epithelium and supports the **mucus barrier**, the layer of mucus that
keeps bacteria away from the epithelial surface. When fibre runs short, however, gut microbes can degrade
that mucus layer for nutrients instead, thinning the barrier; this has been shown in gnotobiotic mice
(germ-free mice colonised with a defined set of bacteria) [@desai2016fibre].

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: not all fibre ferments the same way
Fibre is the substrate here (its chemistry is in the [*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd)
chapter); for the microbiome, what matters is how fermentable it is. Rapidly fermented soluble fibres
(inulin in onion and garlic, pectin in fruit, β-glucan in oats) give a prompt burst of SCFAs and gas.
Resistant starch, in cooked-and-cooled rice or pasta, slightly green bananas and legumes, ferments more
slowly and further along the colon, and is relatively **butyrogenic** (it yields a higher proportion of
butyrate) [@topping2001rs]. The variety of fibre matters as well as the quantity.
:::

### Vitamins made in the gut, and why the host gains little {#sec-vitamins}

Gut microbes synthesise vitamins, but little of this reaches the host, because nearly all the synthesis
happens in the colon, downstream of where those vitamins are absorbed. The vitamins concerned are vitamin
K2 (menaquinones) and several B vitamins (biotin, folate, riboflavin and B12).

Vitamin B12 is the clearest example. Most gut microbes are net consumers of B12, and the little they
make is produced beyond the terminal ileum, the site where B12 (bound to intrinsic factor) is absorbed
(see the *Digestion and absorption* chapter). Colonic microbial B12 is therefore essentially unavailable
to the host, and dietary B12 from animal sources remains the functional supply [@degnan2014b12].
Bacterial K2 is similarly poorly available, and diet remains the principal source of vitamin K
[@lai2022vitk]. The vitamins themselves are covered in the
[*Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) chapter; the principle
here is that "made in the gut" does not mean "available to the host".

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: butyrate is the least abundant SCFA. Why does losing it matter more to the colon than losing acetate?
Butyrate is the colonocytes' main fuel and supports the mucus barrier, so the colon depends on it
locally. Acetate, although more abundant, is poorly extracted in the gut and travels systemically to
peripheral tissues. Abundance is not the same as local importance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a vegan patient hopes her gut bacteria will supply her vitamin B12. Why can't they?
B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum, but colonic bacteria make it further along, in the colon, and
most gut microbes consume more B12 than they make. Microbial B12 therefore does not reach her
circulation, and she needs a dietary or supplemental source.
:::

## Feeding and shaping the microbiome {#sec-gut-diet}

### How diet shapes it: fibre diversity {#sec-feeding}

Diet is the dominant, fast-acting and reversible influence on the microbiome. When people switch
between an animal-based and a plant-based diet, their microbial community shifts within a single day,
but it reverts within days of a return to their usual diet, and each person's characteristic community
largely persists [@david2014diet]. Diet is therefore an ongoing influence, renewed at every meal, and
not a one-time reprogramming.

The variety of plants eaten matters more than any single food. People who eat the widest variety of plants
tend to have the most diverse microbiomes. A memorable but unproven heuristic from citizen science is
"about 30 different plant types a week", a target for variety that counts wholegrains, legumes, nuts,
seeds, fruit and vegetables [@mcdonald2018american].

The opposite pattern, a chronically low-fibre "Western" diet, deprives fibre-fermenting bacteria of
substrate and lowers diversity. The most dramatic version of this, a loss of diversity that becomes irreversible over
generations, comes from mice, so the evidence for that extreme is limited, though the direction of the
effect is well supported [@sonnenburg2016diet]. Whole dietary patterns such as the Mediterranean diet are
associated with more SCFA producers and with less frailty and inflammation [@ghosh2020mediterranean]
(see the [*What a healthy diet looks like*](dietary-guidelines-patterns.qmd) chapter).

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating for the gut microbiome in Singapore
The main dietary change is greater fibre variety, and Singapore's food offers easy swaps:

- Replace white rice with brown, red or mixed rice some of the time.
- Choose wholemeal over white bread.
- Add legumes and dhal, thunder-tea rice (*lei cha*), tofu and more vegetables.
- Keep the skins on fruit and potatoes.

Aim for many different plants across the week, not one "gut superfood". Only about 4% of the staples
eaten in Singapore are wholegrain, so most people have plenty of room to add wholegrains (see
[The Singapore picture](#sec-singapore)).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 Healthy kitchen: go gradual, and keep the fluids
A sudden increase in fibre means a sudden increase in fermentation, and the result is gas and
bloating (harmless, but unpleasant). Increase fibre gradually over a couple of weeks and drink enough
water. Cooking and then cooling starchy foods (rice, potatoes, pasta) forms resistant starch, a slowly
fermented, butyrogenic fibre, in foods such as cold rice or potato salad.
:::

### Probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics and postbiotics: consensus definitions {#sec-biotics}

The products marketed for the microbiome have precise consensus definitions from the International
Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP):

| Term | Definition (ISAPP) | In plain terms |
|---|---|---|
| Probiotic | "Live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit" [@hill2014probiotic] | Live, defined, dosed microbes shown to do something |
| Prebiotic | "A substrate selectively used by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit" [@gibson2017prebiotic] | Food for beneficial gut microbes (mostly fibres) |
| Synbiotic | A probiotic + prebiotic combination [@swanson2020synbiotic] | The microbes and their food together |
| Postbiotic | A preparation of inanimate microbes and/or their components [@salminen2021postbiotic] | The beneficial products, with no live microbes |

::: {.callout-important}
## Is every fermented food a probiotic?
Fermented foods are often assumed to deliver live, beneficial microbes. A **fermented food** is
defined by its process, "made through desired microbial growth and enzymatic conversions", and not by
the microbes present when it is eaten [@marco2021fermented]. Many fermented foods are cooked or
pasteurised before eating (tempeh, bread, most miso once boiled), so they carry few or no live
microbes. They remain good foods. A small, short Stanford trial found that a high-fermented-food diet
raised microbial diversity and lowered inflammatory markers where a high-fibre diet did not; that
result is a hypothesis to test, not a basis for prescribing [@wastyk2021diet]. Only a defined, dosed,
live product meets the definition of a probiotic.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: after a plant-based week, a patient finds her microbiome has drifted back. Was the week wasted?
No. Diet shifts the community within a day, but the community reverts within days of a return to the
usual diet, so the effect lasts only as long as the eating pattern does. Diet is an ongoing influence,
renewed at every meal, which is why the advice is a sustained variety of plants.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient says the tempeh she eats every day is a probiotic. Is it?
No. A probiotic must deliver live, defined microbes in a dose shown to benefit health, whereas a
fermented food is defined by how it was made. Tempeh is cooked before it is eaten, so it carries few or
no live microbes. It is still a good food.
:::

## Clinical problems and unproven claims {#sec-gut-clinical}

::: {.spectrum}
[Evidence for microbiome interventions]{.tree-title}

- Test kits for well people: no proven clinical action
- Psychobiotics for mood: small or preclinical effects
- Probiotics with antibiotics: modest, strain-specific benefit
- FMT for recurrent *C. difficile*: about 81% cured by one infusion

[No proven benefit]{.spectrum-end} [Proven benefit]{.spectrum-end}
:::

### Antibiotics, *C. difficile* and faecal microbiota transplant {#sec-clinical}

Broad-spectrum antibiotics disturb the whole ecosystem, because they act on the wider community as well
as on the pathogen. The result is **dysbiosis** (disruption of the normal microbial community) and
often **antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (AAD)**. Recovery can be incomplete, with some species still
missing months later [@palleja2018recovery]. The most dangerous consequence is **_Clostridioides
difficile_ infection**, in which a depleted microbiome allows this toxin-producing bacterium to
proliferate and cause severe colitis.

Probiotics given with antibiotics help modestly, and only in specific settings. They produce a modest,
strain-dependent reduction in AAD and *C. difficile* risk in higher-risk settings, but the evidence does
not support a blanket rule of "probiotics with every antibiotic", and there is a counter-signal that
probiotics can delay recovery of the native microbiome afterwards [@goldenberg2017cdi;
@suez2018probiotic]. (The AGA guideline addresses probiotics for *C. difficile* prevention during
antibiotic treatment; the AAD benefit comes from a Cochrane review, a related but distinct question
[@agaProbiotics2020].) When a patient on antibiotics asks whether to take a probiotic, you can explain
that any benefit is modest and strain-specific; the prescribing decision belongs to the treating team.

::: {.callout-note}
## FMT: restoring a whole ecosystem
The clearest evidence that the microbiome behaves as an ecosystem comes from **faecal microbiota
transplant (FMT)**, the transfer of stool from a healthy donor to restore a depleted community. For
recurrent *C. difficile* infection it is highly effective. A landmark trial was stopped early because
FMT cured about 81% of patients after one infusion (~94% with a repeat) against roughly 31% with the
antibiotic alone [@vannood2013fmt]. Two microbiota products are now FDA-approved (Rebyota in 2022;
Vowst, the first oral product, in 2023) [@fda2022rebyota; @fda2023vowst]. FMT is proven only for
recurrent *C. difficile* infection, not for obesity, irritable bowel syndrome, autism or "wellness",
and it carries a real risk of transmitting infection: a 2019 safety alert followed a fatal
transmission [@fmt2019safety]. **Recognise it and refer: FMT is a medical therapy with one narrow
indication.**
:::

### Microbiome claims and the evidence {#sec-hype}

Three claims about the microbiome are common in consumer marketing:

- "A microbiome test kit shows how healthy your gut is." For a well person, it does not. There is
  no agreed "healthy" reference microbiome, reproducibility is poor (the same stool can give different
  results from different companies), and no proven clinical action follows from the result.
  International consensus discourages these tests without a medical indication; the money is better
  spent on more plants [@porcari2024microbiometest].
- "A detox or cleanse resets your microbiome." There is no accumulated toxin to flush out, and a
  low-fibre juice cleanse provides little substrate for gut microbes. The only intervention in medicine
  that resets the community is FMT, for its one narrow indication.
- "The gut is your second brain: gut serotonin controls your mood." The gut does make about 90–95% of
  the body's serotonin, but that serotonin regulates gut motility, and peripheral serotonin does not
  cross the blood–brain barrier [@serotoninGutReview]. The metaphor has no mechanism behind it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The gut–brain axis: real channel, cautious claims
There is a genuine **gut–brain axis**, the two-way signalling between the gut and the brain: the
microbiome can signal to the brain through the vagus nerve, SCFAs, the immune system and microbial
neuroactive metabolites [@cryan2019microbiota]. The most striking results, in which transplanted
microbes change behaviour, come largely from mouse studies, and the benefits of **psychobiotics**
(microbes or microbial products claimed to improve mental health) for mood in humans are mostly small
or preclinical. The channel is real; the mood claims are unproven. Its role in appetite and behaviour
is taken up in the [*Appetite and weight regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd) chapter.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a well patient asks for faecal microbiota transplant to help them lose weight. What do you tell them, and why?
FMT is proven for one indication, recurrent *C. difficile* infection, where it restores a depleted
community. It is not proven for obesity, and it carries a real risk of transmitting infection. Explain
this, and refer any genuine indication to a specialist rather than treating FMT as a wellness reset.
:::

## How should a patient eat for a healthy microbiome? {#sec-close}

The evidence points to a pattern of eating, not to a product:

- A wide variety of plants across the week (wholegrains, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts and seeds),
  because diverse fibres feed a diverse, resilient microbiome that yields SCFAs.
- Fermented foods, for those who enjoy them, including some with live cultures.
- A gradual increase in fibre, with fluids.
- No test kits, cleanses or microbiome supplements, none of which has a proven benefit for a well
  person.

The microbiome is maintained by habitual diet, what is eaten every day.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

**Fibre intake in Singapore is low.** Only about 4% of the staples eaten in Singapore are wholegrain,
against a target of about 30%, and average fibre intake is below the Health Promotion Board's
recommendation (around 20 g/day for women and 26 g/day for men) [@mohNNS2022]. Most of the population
eats too little fibre to supply its fibre-fermenting bacteria, which is why the food-first swaps in
[How diet shapes it: fibre diversity](#sec-feeding) are a worthwhile change for most people.

**Local fermented foods illustrate the live-versus-cooked distinction.** Fermented foods run through
Singapore's food cultures, and they divide along the line that matters for the probiotic definition:
those eaten with live cultures and those cooked first.

| Still has live cultures (eaten raw/unheated) | Cooked → few or no live microbes (still good foods) |
|---|---|
| Kimchi, unpasteurised *achar*, Yakult / cultured-milk drinks, kombucha | Tempeh, *taucheo* (fermented soybean paste), *belacan*, fish sauce, miso once boiled |

Different organisms ferment each food:

- Tempeh uses a mould, *Rhizopus*.
- *Natto* uses *Bacillus subtilis*, which makes it a notable source of vitamin K2 (see
  [the vitamin section](#sec-vitamins)).
- Miso and *taucheo* use *koji* mould (*Aspergillus oryzae*).
- Kimchi uses lactic-acid bacteria.

*Tapai* (fermented rice or tapioca) contains a few per cent alcohol, which matters for Muslim patients.
*Yong tau foo*, a common confusion, is not a fermented food.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 Keep the cultures alive
To keep live cultures, add them off the heat: stir miso into soup after it stops boiling, eat *achar*
and kimchi unheated, and treat cultured-milk drinks as the live option. A cooked ferment (tempeh, most
*taucheo*) is still a nutritious food; it simply delivers few live microbes.
:::

**Yakult has some evidence, but no proven broad benefit.** Cultured-milk drinks are a daily habit in
many Singaporean families. The bacterium in Yakult (*Lactobacillus casei* Shirota) survives transit
through the gut and has some signals from small trials, but the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
rejected its broad health claims for lack of convincing evidence [@efsa2010lcs;
@katokataoka2016lcs]. It is a reasonable drink (watch the sugar); it is not a treatment. A marketed
benefit is not the same as a proven benefit.

**There is no single "Singaporean" microbiome.** A large local multi-ethnic study found no
predominant microbiome type across the community, a close-to-home illustration that variation between
individuals is the rule, and that diet and lifestyle, not nationality, shape the community
[@khine2021multiethnic]. Vegetarian and vegan eating is common in several local communities, so the
fact that gut bacteria cannot supply B12 has practical consequences here: when you take a diet history
from a vegetarian or vegan patient, ask about a dietary or supplemental B12 source (see the
*Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes* chapter).
